vignette:
Mark, at 39, carries the weight of a life that feels fundamentally altered. Before that day, he was a man grounded in his work, proud of his skill with his hands, and steady in his routines. He'd been a construction foreman for over a decade, overseeing crews, ensuring safety, and always priding himself on a job well done. He was married then, and while not perfect, his life felt predictable, solid, much like the foundations he helped lay.

The shift happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday, a day that now feels burned into his memory. They were on a downtown high-rise project, a complex pour on the 20th floor. He remembers the hum of the concrete pump, the rhythmic clang of rebar, the usual symphony of a busy site. Then, the sound changed - a sudden, violent screech of twisting metal, unlike anything he'd ever heard. He looked up just as the section of scaffolding where John, a young apprentice he'd been mentoring, was working buckled. The world seemed to slow down. He saw the sheer terror on John's face, the desperate grab for something that wasn't there, and then the sickening plummet. The impact, when it came, was a sound Mark knows he will carry forever, echoing the finality of it all. He was frozen, adrenaline coursing through him, watching the chaos erupt, the frantic calls, the rush of emergency services. He remembers the smell of dust and something metallic, and the profound, cold shock that settled deep in his bones.

In the immediate aftermath, Mark felt a peculiar kind of numbness. He went through the motions, answering questions, giving his statement, but it was like watching himself from a distance. He tried to go back to work the next day, convincing himself he needed to be strong, to show his crew he was okay. But the site was different. Every loud bang, every distant siren, every time he looked up at the skeletal structure of the building, his stomach clenched. He started avoiding the upper floors, delegating tasks he used to relish. The smell of fresh concrete, once a comforting scent of progress, now brought a metallic tang to his mouth, a phantom echo of that day.

Weeks turned into months, and the numbness began to crack, replaced by a relentless current of anxiety and guilt. Sleep became a battleground. He wakes up most nights, his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, the image of John falling replaying in vivid, horrific detail. Sometimes, it's not even an image, just the sound - that terrible, twisting screech - that jolts him awake. During the day, intrusive thoughts ambush him. He'll be measuring a beam, and suddenly he's back on that platform, analyzing, replaying, asking himself a thousand times what he could have done differently, even though logically he knows there was nothing. He feels a crushing weight of responsibility, a belief that he somehow failed John, failed to keep him safe.

His marriage started to unravel. He became withdrawn, irritable. His wife would ask what was wrong, and he'd snap, or just grunt, unable to articulate the churning dread inside him. He stopped going out, stopped enjoying their weekend hikes. He found himself avoiding his old friends from work, unable to tolerate their casual talk, their laughter. He started taking longer routes to work, just to avoid seeing other construction sites, the towering cranes, the familiar orange safety netting that now felt like a cruel joke. He just wanted to be left alone, but even then, he felt profoundly lonely, disconnected from everyone, including himself.

Now, eighteen months later, Mark is divorced. His wife eventually left, exhausted by his emotional distance and volatile moods. He still works in construction, but it's a constant struggle. The noise of heavy machinery is a perpetual trigger, making him jump, his muscles tensing. He's hypervigilant, scanning every corner of a site, every piece of equipment, convinced something else is about to go wrong. He can't shake the feeling of impending doom. He's often exhausted, the lack of sleep catching up with him, but he can't rest. He drinks a few beers most nights, hoping it will dull the edges, but it only makes his sleep more fragmented, his mornings more bleak. He feels like a stranger in his own body, haunted by a past he can't escape, living in a present that offers little solace. He just wants to feel like himself again, the man who used to enjoy building things, the man who could sleep through the night.
